objectives: Tell the landside of an airport from the airside and know which side you are on.
Read the main signs and recognise the difference between departure, arrival and transfer.
Pass security and passport control knowing what you will be asked and what you may carry.
Find your gate, your free time and your luggage after a flight.
Make a connection between two flights without missing it.
Ask for help in a way that gets you a real answer.
Recover a lost, delayed or misrouted bag when it happens.

sections.body:
An airport is a machine for moving strangers to the right place at the right time. It looks like one enormous building, but it is easier to read once you understand that it has two halves.

The **landside** is the public half: the road, the car park, the check-in desks, the ticket machines, the café before the security check. Anyone can walk in. The **airside** is the secure half: the gates, the shops, the lounges, the air bridges. You can only enter it after the security check, and you leave it again at passport control on arrival.

Inside the airside, the building is divided into **terminals** and then into **concourses**, which are long arms of the building full of gates. Your flight leaves from a **gate**, a door onto the aircraft, and the gate is the one piece of information you must find and remember. Gates are numbered, and the number tells you the group: A12 is in concourse A, terminal 2 usually means a different building from terminal 1.

Airports are also built in layers, and the layers have names. The **terminal** is the building. The **floor** matters: in many airports departures are on the upper floor and arrivals on the lower, because arriving passengers need to come up to the street while departing passengers need to get down to the coaches. The **piers** are the long arms with aircraft parked along both sides. And the shops, cafés and lounges are the reason a long wait does not have to be a punishment.

Airports are large because they were built for the peak of the last century, when bags were checked at a counter, every seat needed a paper ticket, and nobody expected a queue for a coffee. Much of what looks confusing today is old space that has been patched with new signs. That is good news: the confusion is in the building, not in you.

There are three journeys inside an airport, and they are always in this order. **Departure** is the trip out: check in, security, passport control, gate. **Arrival** is the trip in: land, passport control, baggage claim, exit. **Transfer** is the trip between two flights at the same airport: you land, follow the transfer signs, and go to another gate without going through the city.

Learn those three words and half the signs in the building already make sense.

Two rhythms run through the building, and knowing them saves you a lot of walking. The **early wave** is the business morning: short flights, short lines, and empty corridors. The **middle of the day** is the wave that hurts, with the afternoon departures, when the security queue stretches round a corner and every café is full. If you can choose your hours, travel outside the peak and the same airport feels twice as small.

And the staff work in shifts, which is why the same question gets a different answer at 09:00 and at 21:00. The information desk knows the flight schedule. The gate agent knows the delay. The baggage handler knows where your bag is. One question, aimed at the right person, saves twenty minutes of walking.
examples: I need the departure halls, not arrivals.
Is this a transfer or do I have to go through customs?
sections.heading: What an airport is, and why it feels confusing

sections.body:
Most of the stress of an airport happens in the two hours before departure, and most of that stress is avoidable. Everything below can be done from home, and each item removes one queue from your day.

**Check in online.** Almost every airline now lets you check in online, which prints or stores the boarding pass on your phone and, for many airlines, lets you drop your bag at a self-service kiosk in under two minutes. Check in opens 24 to 48 hours before departure and closes 60 to 90 minutes before it. The exact window is on your ticket, and the airline's app is faster and clearer than the airport website.

**Choose your seat and get the boarding pass.** Boarding passes are issued in waves. Usually the first group boards for people who need extra time, have bought extra luggage, or are in a loyalty programme. The last group is usually the one that boards with overhead lockers full. If you would rather not fight for the overhead locker, buy a seat near the front of the zone, or check a bag and travel with nothing to store.

**Check the terminal and the gate.** The terminal is fixed on your ticket and rarely changes. The gate is not: it is assigned later, often the evening before, and it can change several times. So check the terminal the night before, and the gate when you arrive at the airport.

**Look up the visa and entry rules now.** They are the one thing that can end a trip at the desk, and they are online, free, and slow to change. Check the destination country's rules and the rules for any country you transit through, including whether you need to collect bags and pass through security again.

**Weigh and measure the bag.** Airline limits are strict, and the bag scales at the airport are the last place you can fix it. A bag that is 1 cm over the limit is refused and sent to the hold at a high price.
examples: I have checked in online and I only need to drop my bag.
Which zone am I in for boarding?
Do I need a visa for this transit country?
sections.heading: What you can settle before the day of the flight

sections.body:
Airport signage is short by design, and the words are always the same in every country that follows the international convention. Learn these and you can move through any airport in Europe, Asia and the Americas.

**Departures** (and **Départs**, **Abflug**, **Salidas**, ** departures** in English) points to the check-in and security side. **Arrivals** points to the side where arriving passengers come out. The two are usually in opposite halves of the building.

**Gates** are lettered and numbered. **Boarding** is the period when you are called to the aircraft, and the board shows the gate, the flight number, the destination and the time. The boarding time is not the departure time: boarding usually starts 30 to 45 minutes before the aircraft leaves.

**Security** or **Screening** is the checkpoint. **Passport control** and **Immigration** are the desks where your passport is checked. **Customs** and **Baggage reclaim** or **Baggage claim** are where you collect your bag and pass the goods declaration.

Two more words cause trouble. **Transfer** or **Connection** means you change aircraft at the same airport; you will see a sign with the flight number of your next flight. **Landside** and **airside** are used less often on signs but appear on every map, and they tell you whether you can leave the building without a ticket.

Three more signs appear before you reach security. **Check-in** or **Bag drop** points to the desks and the kiosks. **Shuttle** or **Terminal transfer** points to the train or bus that carries you between buildings. And **Information** is a desk marked with a lowercase i, where a person will look up your flight, tell you which terminal to use, and sometimes walk you there.

Finally, one word appears in every language and always means the same thing: **exit**. It points out of the building, and in an airport it is not the way to the gate. Many travellers follow the nearest EXIT sign and end up in the car park. Inside the building, the way to the gate is never the way out.
examples: Gate B22, boarding at 14:35.
I have a transfer to flight QR 852.
Baggage claim, belt 7.
sections.heading: The words that appear on every airport sign

terms.example: Show your boarding pass at the gate and find your seat.
terms.gloss: The card or phone screen that lets you board the aircraft. It carries your name, the flight, the gate, the seat and the boarding time.

terms.example: My flight is delayed, so I am stuck in the transit area.
terms.gloss: The secure part of the airport where you wait for a connecting flight. You cannot leave it without a new ticket.

terms.example: My gate has changed from B22 to C4.
terms.gloss: The door onto the aircraft, identified by a letter and a number, for example B22. It is assigned late and can change.

terms.example: Your bag is on belt 7, and it has been there for ten minutes.
terms.gloss: The area where the belt for your flight delivers your suitcase. The belt number is shown on the screens above it.

terms.example: I have a two-hour transfer in Singapore.
terms.gloss: A connection between two flights at the same airport, without going through the city in between.

sections.body:
This is the departure route, and the order is the same in almost every airport in the world. If you follow the departure signs, you will not need to ask a single question.

The first decision is whether you have already checked in and have a boarding pass. If you do, you skip the desks. If you do not, the check-in desks or the self-service kiosks are the first stop, and your bag goes on the belt there.

Then the security check, then passport control for international flights, then the gate. Between the last two there is usually a long corridor with shops, and that corridor is where people get lost, because it looks like a shopping centre and not like a way to a gate.

Watch the screens, not the boards, once you are past security. The boards list many flights; the screens list the ones close to you and tell you the walking time to each gate. The walking time is printed on purpose: if the screen says 18 minutes, you should be at the gate in 18 minutes, and boarding usually closes 20 minutes before departure.

Two habits make the difference between a smooth journey and a bad one. First, keep your boarding pass and passport in your hand, not in a bag that goes on a belt. Second, allow time for the things that are not in the walking time: the queue at security, the walk through the corridor, and a passport desk that has twelve people in front of you.

And if the boarding time is close, do not walk. Follow the staff and the signs for the nearest gate, take the shuttle if it is faster, and call the airline if the desk has not opened yet. An hour of stress saved is worth the ten minutes you spent reading this.
examples: I have checked in, so I only need to drop this bag.
Am I allowed to keep this laptop in my hand bag?
How long does it take to walk to gate C4?
sections.heading: From the aircraft door to the gate, in the right order
steps: Arrive at the terminal two to three hours before an international flight.
Check in and print or open your boarding pass.
Drop your checked bag at the desk or the kiosk and keep the receipt.
Pass through security with your boarding pass and passport in your hand.
Pass passport control if the flight crosses a border.
Follow the signs and the screens to your gate.
Be at the gate 30 minutes before boarding and watch the desk for changes.

sections.body:
Airport signage is short by design, and the same icons are used across countries. They are drawn from a small international set.

Look for the **aeroplane taking off** icon for departures and the **aeroplane landing** icon for arrivals. The **passport** icon means passport control. A **suitcase on a belt** means baggage claim. A **trolley with a case** means bag drop and check-in. An **arrow** means direction, and an arrow with a **staircase** or a **lift** means a change of level.

Two conventions catch people out. Yellow or black-on-yellow signs usually mark **transfers and border control**, so if you are transferring you look for a yellow sign. And a pictogram on the floor is a **queue marker**: stand on it and you will be served there.

Numbers on signs are usually walking times in minutes. A sign reading "Gates D4–D20, 12 min" is not a distance in kilometres; it is a promise about how long the walk takes if you go now.

The colours carry meaning too, in most airports. Black and white on yellow is the international warning colour, used for anything that concerns safety or the border. Blue is for services that are not flights, such as toilets, lifts and information. Green marks the way out and the emergency exits. And every sign is written in the local language first, with English or a pictogram beside it, which is why the pictogram matters more than the word.

One more icon worth learning is the **staircase with a downward arrow next to an aeroplane**. That is the shuttle train or bus that runs between terminals, and it is the answer whenever the sign says your gate is in another terminal. Taking it usually takes less time than walking, and it is the only way to get to some remote gates at all.
examples: The passport symbol means I need to go through border control here.
Twelve minutes to the gates, so I should go now.
sections.heading: The pictograms that carry the meaning

symbols.meaning: Aeroplane taking off: the departures side of the building.
Aeroplane landing: the arrivals side of the building.
Open passport with a stamp: passport control or immigration.
Suitcase on a moving belt: baggage claim.
Trolley with a case: check-in and bag drop.
A number beside an arrow: the walking time to the destination, in minutes.

sections.body:
The security check exists to make sure nothing dangerous goes into the aircraft. It is also the part of the journey most likely to be new to you, because the rules on what you may carry differ by country and by airport. The standard in most countries is the same.

**Liquids.** In most airports you may carry a container of liquid up to 100 ml, and the container must fit in a clear bag of about one litre. That means a 200 ml bottle of shampoo is not allowed, and a full 1.5 litre bottle of water is not allowed. The rule does not apply to medicines, to food for babies, or to the ice packs that come with a delivery. Some airports have separate lanes with different limits, so read the sign before you queue.

**Sharp objects.** Knives, scissors, tools, razors and matches are not allowed in hand baggage. Nails, small make-up, and the tools in a repair kit are allowed in most countries.

**Electronics.** You will be asked to take your laptop, your phone and your large tablet out and put them in a separate tray. Keep them with you. Do not lock a phone into a checked bag; the screen can be opened and inspected, and if the battery is swollen it cannot travel at all.

**The screening itself.** You put your bag on the belt, remove your belt and watch, and you walk through a metal detector or a body scanner. The officer may ask you to step aside and answer a few questions, or to open a bag. If the officer asks to see something, they will point at it; you can open your own bag.

**Keep your documents.** Passport, boarding pass and travel documents go in your hand bag, not in the checked one. If they are in your checked bag and the bag goes to the wrong country, you are stuck.
examples: Do I need to take my laptop out of the bag?
I have medication, and I am taking it in my hand bag.
Can I keep my water bottle if I empty it?
sections.heading: Security, and what you will be asked to do

terms.example: Security screening starts at the end of this corridor.
terms.gloss: The checkpoint where bags and people are checked before entering the secure part of the airport.

terms.example: My bottle is 500 ml, so I have to empty it before screening.
terms.gloss: The rule limiting containers of liquid in hand baggage, usually to 100 ml each in a clear bag.

sections.body:
**Passport control** is the desk where an officer checks that you are allowed to enter the country. At departure it confirms you are allowed to leave; at arrival it confirms you are allowed to come in. The queue is usually the longest in the building, and it is usually longer for a foreign passport than for a national one.

At the desk you show your passport, and sometimes your boarding pass. You may be asked for the **purpose of your visit**, how long you are staying, and where you are staying. Answer briefly and honestly. If your accommodation is booked, the booking reference is useful; if you are staying with a friend, their address and name are useful. If you are travelling on a visa, keep the visa page and any printed approval with you, because the officer may want to see it.

After arrival, follow the **arrivals** signs, not the departures signs. The order is: passport control first, then **baggage claim**, then **customs**, then the exit.

At baggage claim, find the belt for your flight on the screen. The belt number is shown next to the flight number, and it is often right next to the number of the belt itself. If your bag is not on the belt, do not wait forever. Note the belt number and go to the baggage services desk, which is usually near the carousel or in the hall. If the bag is genuinely lost, you file a report there, and you keep the receipts for anything you must buy to travel.

Customs is usually a walk through a channel marked **nothing to declare**, with a separate red channel for people with goods to declare. Saying "no" when you have nothing to declare takes five seconds.
examples: I am here for ten days, and I am staying in a hotel in the city centre.
Here is my visa approval and my accommodation booking.
My bag is not on belt 7. Where is the baggage services desk?
sections.heading: Passport control, and getting your bag back

terms.example: Passport control is straight ahead, and baggage claim is on the left.
terms.gloss: The border desk where an officer checks your passport and your right to enter or leave the country.

terms.example: Do I go through the red channel if I bought two bottles of wine?
terms.gloss: The place where you declare goods over the allowance. Most travellers use the green or white channel for nothing to declare.

sections.body:
A transfer means you land at one airport and leave again on another aircraft, often in another terminal, sometimes in another country. The good news is that you do not normally go through customs, because you never leave the airport. The bad news is that a transfer can be tight.

Follow the **transfer** or **connections** signs as soon as you leave the aircraft. These signs are usually yellow or brown, and they usually show a flight number rather than a gate number. If the staff at the aircraft door point you somewhere, follow them: at many airports the transfer route is the opposite direction from the arrivals route, which is exactly where you would guess.

Check the transfer time honestly. A connection under 60 minutes is possible between two flights at a large airport and impossible at a small one, because you may have to change terminals and go through a second security check. Many airlines set a **minimum connection time** of 60 to 90 minutes for that reason, and if you book a shorter one they will not protect you when you miss it.

Two things can break a transfer. The first is a delay on the first flight, which is the airline's problem and usually its duty to rebook you. The second is a **connection check**: some airports, and some airlines, require you to collect your checked bag at baggage claim and take it through security again. This happens at airports where the transit area is not secure, and it adds 45 minutes. Check the airport's rules for your specific route before you fly.

If you are delayed, go to the transfer desk of your airline as soon as you land, before you start walking. They can rebook you onto a later flight faster than the app can, and they can see options you cannot.
examples: I have a connection to flight BA 286. Which way is the transfer route?
Do I need to collect my bag and go through security again?
My first flight was delayed. Can you put me on the next one?
sections.heading: Making a transfer without missing it

sections.body:
**Wrong half of the building.** Arrivals and departures are often on opposite sides, and a wrong turn can cost you twenty minutes. Check the sign before you move.

**Ignoring the walking time on the screen.** It is there so you can decide. A screen that says 25 minutes to a gate means the walk is long and boarding may already be open.

**Waiting for the gate to be announced early.** Gates are assigned late, and the one on your old boarding pass may be wrong. Look at the screens from time to time, not once.

**Losing the board without noticing.** The gate number is on the boarding pass, but the boarding time and the gate can both change. Take a photograph of the board, and set an alarm for boarding time minus ten minutes.

**Missing the last security check.** Some airports close security for a flight before the aircraft leaves. If the walk to your gate is long, you may have to go through security twice, and the second queue is not counted in the walking time.
sections.heading: The five ways travellers get lost

sections.body:
You will need help eventually, and the quality of the answer depends on the question. Staff at airports are trained, but they cannot see your ticket.

Start with the one fact that identifies your situation: the flight number and the destination. "I am on flight LH 411 to Frankfurt, and I cannot find gate B14" is a good question. "Where is gate B14?" is a bad one, because the answer may be a shrug.

Say who you are, in one clause, when it matters. "I have a connecting flight in 45 minutes" is the sentence that changes how fast somebody helps you. "I am a Vietnamese citizen travelling on a business visa" tells the officer what documents to expect.

If you do not understand the answer, do not nod and walk away. Say that you did not understand and ask again in simpler words: "Sorry, can you say that again more slowly?" or "Can you write it down?" An airport has paper, and writing the answer down is how you avoid a second trip to the same desk.

If you are lost, do not ask a random traveller first. Ask a member of staff in uniform, or go to an information desk marked with an i. Staff know the building; travellers do not.

And when the delay is not your fault, keep the record. Take the name of the agent, keep the boarding pass, and photograph the screens that show the delay. Airlines release compensation for cancellations and long delays under the rules that apply in the country of departure, and the first thing they will ask for is evidence.
examples: I am on flight QR 851 to Doha, and I cannot find gate C4.
Sorry, I did not understand. Can you say it again more slowly?
I have a connecting flight in 45 minutes. Can you help me?
sections.heading: What to say when the plan breaks

item.summary: An airport looks like one big building until you try to find a gate in it. After reading this you can read the signs, follow the process in the right order, transfer between flights without panic, and ask the right question when the plan breaks.
item.title: Navigating an Airport Without Getting Lost
